en: The Apadāna of the Elder Citakapūjaka Suvaṇṇabibbohana Chapter 7 I was a king named Mahinda, ruling over the earth. At that time, I had a son, a prince named Jotipāla. He was handsome, possessed of great beauty, and endowed with all the marks of excellence. Seeing him, I was filled with joy; he was like a lotus flower. Then, having gone to the Himālayas, I saw the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World, the Fully Enlightened One, the One Endowed with the Ten Powers. Having approached him, I paid homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One, and sat down to one side, desiring to hear the Dhamma. There, seated to one side, I spoke these words to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, this son of mine, Jotipāla, is very dear to me. May the Blessed One please grant him the going-forth; may the Sugata ordain him. Then the Blessed One, the Great Sage, the Teacher of the World, the Fully Enlightened One, the One Endowed with the Ten Powers, having understood my request, ordained Jotipāla, and taught him the Dhamma that leads to the destruction of suffering. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, the Fully Enlightened One, Jotipāla, with a mind full of faith, attained the fruit of stream-entry. Then, having paid homage to the Blessed One, the Fully Enlightened One, he departed from that place, his purpose accomplished. Later, when I passed away from that human existence, I was reborn in the realm of the Thirty-three gods. There, for a long time, I enjoyed the splendor of the devas, dwelling in celestial palaces, radiant and glorious. When my lifespan there had come to an end, I passed away from that divine existence and was reborn among humans. In every birth, I was wealthy and prosperous, possessing great power and authority, and free from disease. For eighty-four thousand aeons, I never fell into the lower realms. Having performed that meritorious deed, I experienced the fruit of that kamma. Now, in my final existence, I have been born as a human being, in a noble family, endowed with great wealth. I am now a monk, having gone forth under the Buddha, and I dwell in the bliss of liberation, free from defilements.

I remember my former births, my various lives throughout the past. Through the power of that meritorious deed, I have attained this state of peace. Thus did the Elder Citakapūjaka speak of his own past deeds, recounting the history of his former lives. Having heard this, those monks were filled with wonder, and they praised the Elder’s words with joyful hearts. Thus ends the Apadāna of the Elder Citakapūjaka, the seventh in the Suvaṇṇabibbohana Chapter.
“On the bank of the Candabhāgā River,
there I saw seven māluva flowers.”
I have worshipped that funeral pyre.
I do not know a state of woe;
this is the fruit of honoring a stupa.
they were seven wheel-turning monarchs endowed with the seven treasures.
[and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed the venerable elder Citakapūjaka spoke these verses.
This is the seventh legend of the elder Citakapūjaka.
